issues.legal_issue: A contractual sum stipulated for breach does not preclude specific performance when it is a penalty securing performance rather than an alternative to performance.
material_facts: The agreement for sale required a party violating its terms to pay a specified sum as a penalty.
The agreement did not state that the seller could choose to pay that sum instead of conveying the property.
issues.conclusion: The penalty clause did not prevent a decree for specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Jammu and Kashmir Specific Relief Act, 1977 (1920 A.D.) permits specific performance of an otherwise enforceable contract despite a sum being named for breach. The Court applied the distinction between a penalty securing performance, liquidated damages, and a sum payable as an alternative to performance discussed in M.L. Devender Singh v. Syed Khaji, relying on Sir Edward Fry’s treatise; it also relied on Prakash Chand v. Angad Lal. A stipulated sum does not by itself displace the presumption referred to in Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as discussed in M.L. Devender Singh.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks an order requiring a party to perform a contract for the transfer of property.
predicates.stipulated_sum_secures_performance: The contract stipulates a sum payable for breach as security for performance.
predicates.contract_does_not_offer_payment_as_an_al: The contract does not give the party an option to pay the stipulated sum instead of performing the transfer.

issues.definition: When a property-transfer contract is the subject of a specific-performance proceeding and its stipulated sum secures performance rather than substitutes for it, the penalty clause does not preclude specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who proves readiness and willingness to perform is not disentitled to specific performance merely because completion was delayed by other co-owners’ refusal to join in the sale.
material_facts: The purchaser pleaded that he was ready and willing to perform and testified that he could pay the consideration.
The purchaser’s testimony about his ability to pay was not challenged in cross-examination, and he had served a notice seeking execution of the sale deed.
The seller stated in his written defence that the deed could not be executed because other co-owners were not prepared to sell, but did not testify.
The purchaser’s suit was within the limitation period, and there was no evidence that the sellers called upon him to complete the transaction.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was found ready and willing to perform, and the asserted delay did not disentitle him to equitable relief.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a purchaser was ready and willing, and whether delay disentitles the purchaser to relief, depends on the evidence. The Court found the purchaser’s pleading and testimony supported readiness and willingness, while the seller’s own written statement attributed non-completion to the other co-owners and was not supported by testimony. The suit was within limitation, and no evidence showed that the sellers had called upon the purchaser to complete the sale.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and purchaser_proved_readiness_and_ability_to_perform and noncompletion_was_attributed_to_other_owners and suit_was_within_limitation and seller_did_not_prove_purchaser_caused_delay

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract for the transfer of property.
predicates.purchaser_proved_readiness_and_ability_t: The purchaser pleaded and gave evidence that the purchaser was ready and able to perform, and that evidence was not undermined.
predicates.noncompletion_was_attributed_to_other_ow: The seller attributed non-completion to other owners’ unwillingness to join in the transfer.
predicates.suit_was_within_limitation: The purchaser brought the suit within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.seller_did_not_prove_purchaser_caused_de: The seller did not provide evidence that the purchaser caused the delay or was called upon to complete but failed to do so.

issues.definition: A purchaser who proves readiness and ability to perform is not disentitled for unreadiness or delay when non-completion is attributed to other owners, the suit is timely, and the seller does not prove that the purchaser caused the delay.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance may be granted for the identifiable share that a contracting seller can convey even though other co-owners did not agree to the sale.
material_facts: The seller agreed to sell land held in the names of himself, his brother, and his minor son.
The brother did not agree to the sale, and no decree was made for his share; the purchaser did not appeal the denial of relief for that share.
The trial court ordered specific performance for the seller’s share, and the High Court also granted relief for the son’s share after finding that the seller owned it beneficially.
The shares were identifiable, and a purchaser of a share could seek partition to have it demarcated.
issues.conclusion: There was no bar to specific performance for the share or shares the contracting seller could convey; the absence of the other co-owner’s agreement did not make the contract indivisible for that purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Jammu and Kashmir Specific Relief Act, 1977 allows a court, in the circumstances it specifies, to direct performance of the part of a contract that a defaulting party can perform. The Court relied on Kartar Singh v. Harjinder Singh, which held that an agreement may be enforced against the co-owner who signed it where that owner’s share is identifiable; such relief is performance of the contract as between the contracting parties, rather than partial performance of the kind addressed by Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. A purchaser of a share may seek partition to have it demarcated.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and contracting_seller_can_convey_an_identifiable_share and other_coowners_did_not_join the_sale and purchaser_confined_claim_to_shares_available_under_the_contract

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract to transfer jointly held property.
predicates.contracting_seller_can_convey_an_identif: The seller who made the agreement owns a share that can be identified and conveyed.
predicates.other_coowners_did_not_join_the_sale: One or more co-owners did not agree to or join in the sale.
predicates.purchaser_confined_claim_to_shares_avail: The purchaser pursued relief for the share or shares available from the contracting seller and did not pursue relief for an unjoining co-owner’s share.

issues.definition: Specific performance may be granted for a contracting seller’s identifiable share when other co-owners did not join the sale and the purchaser confines the claim to the shares available under the contract.

issues.legal_issue: A conditional statutory restriction on alienating orchard land does not bar a specific-performance decree when the required permission can be sought at the transfer stage.
material_facts: The agreement concerned land that was an orchard when the agreement was made.
The agrarian reform legislation excluded orchards from its relevant definitions of land.
The legislation restricting orchard alienation required prior permission for transfers beyond a specified exception; it did not impose an absolute prohibition.
The statutory objection was raised on appeal long after the suit began, and the Court found it unsupported on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The restriction did not prevent the court from granting specific performance; any required permission could be sought when giving effect to the decree and executing the transfer.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(4) and 2(5) of the Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1972 excluded qualifying orchards from the relevant definition of land; the corresponding definitions were in Sections 2(9) and 2(10) of the Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1976. Section 3(1)(a) of the Jammu and Kashmir Prohibition on Conversion of Land and Alienation of Orchards Act, 1975 imposed a conditional restriction requiring prior permission, subject to an exception, rather than an absolute bar. The Court relied on Bai Dosabai v. Mathuradas Govinddas for the proposition that a decree may be moulded to account for a statutory restriction on alienation.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract to transfer property.
predicates.property_qualifies_as_orchard: The property is an orchard within the relevant statutory definitions.
predicates.transfer_restriction_requires_permission: The restriction permits transfer if a required permission is obtained, rather than prohibiting transfer absolutely.
predicates.permission_can_be_sought_when_transfer_i: The required permission can be sought when the transfer is carried out under the decree.

issues.definition: A conditional restriction on transfer does not bar a specific-performance decree when the property is an orchard and the required permission can be sought at the time of transfer.

issues.legal_issue: An unrebutted finding that property named in a minor child’s name was purchased with the parent’s funds may support specific performance against the share held in the child’s name.
material_facts: The agreement stated that the seller had purchased a share of the land in the name of his minor son.
The High Court found that the seller had purchased that share with his own funds and was its actual owner.
The defendants led no evidence to rebut that finding, and the son did not testify after attaining majority to controvert the purchaser’s evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no basis to interfere with the finding that the seller owned the share in the son’s name, and upheld specific performance for that share.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the ownership question as one of evidence. Given the agreement’s statement that the share was purchased in the minor’s name, the evidence that the seller supplied the purchase money, and the absence of rebuttal evidence, the finding of the lower courts could not be regarded as erroneous so as to warrant appellate interference.

rule.if: appeal_from_specific_performance_decree and property_is_named_in_minor_childs_name and parent_supplied_purchase_funds and ownership_evidence_was_not_rebutted

predicates.appeal_from_specific_performance_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree granting specific performance of a property-transfer contract.
predicates.property_is_named_in_minor_childs_name: The property or share is recorded or described as being in a minor child’s name.
predicates.parent_supplied_purchase_funds: Evidence shows that the parent supplied the funds used to acquire the property or share.
predicates.ownership_evidence_was_not_rebutted: The opposing parties provided no evidence rebutting the evidence that the parent funded the purchase.

issues.definition: When property in a minor child’s name was purchased with a parent’s funds and that evidence is unrebutted, the finding of parental ownership may be upheld for specific performance.
